scenes.narration: Lipid bilayers are nearly impermeable to ions and most polar molecules, and the reason is energetic, not a simple matter of size. Crossing the hydrophobic core means shedding the shell of water an ion or polar group wears, and stripping that water off costs a lot of energy. Hydrophobicity is the key variable. Indole, the uncharged ring of tryptophan, slips through a membrane far more easily than tryptophan itself, even though the ring is nearly the same. Charge is the toll. Across the whole range, permeability spans about 12 orders of magnitude.

scenes.narration: Membrane transport proteins sort into three families by speed and energy source. Channels are the fastest, up to about 10 million ions per second, but passive. They only let things move down their gradient, with selectivity built into their structure. Carriers are slower and can be regulated. They change shape to ferry their cargo across. Pumps are the slowest, around 100 cycles per second, but they spend ATP to push molecules against their gradient. Speed, regulation, and energy source together tell you which machine you are looking at.

scenes.narration: The potassium channel moves ions at remarkable speed using a simple trick: electrostatic repulsion. Several potassium ions sit in the selectivity filter at once, across four binding sites, S1 through S4. Because like charges repel, the arrival of one ion shoves the ion ahead of it out the far side, like balls knocking down an assembly line, or a Newton's cradle. That knock-on turns binding energy directly into exit energy, so the channel is selective and fast at the same time, passing potassium at near the diffusion limit.

scenes.narration: Secondary active transport comes in two flavors, and both spend the sodium gradient the pump builds. Symporters move two species in the same direction, SGLT1 in the intestine drags glucose uphill by riding sodium downhill. Antiporters move them in opposite directions, the cardiac sodium-calcium exchanger pushes calcium out using the inward sodium flow. Neither one burns ATP directly; they borrow the energy stored in the sodium gradient like a waterwheel stealing energy from a current. Every one of them ultimately depends on the sodium-potassium pump.

scenes.narration: Here is a practical decision tree for classifying any transport event. First ask whether the molecule needs to cross at all, and whether it is small and nonpolar. If so, it simply diffuses, like oxygen into a red blood cell. If it needs help, ask which direction it moves relative to its gradient. Downhill through a protein is facilitated diffusion or a channel. Uphill means active transport, powered directly by ATP in a pump, or indirectly by an ion gradient in secondary active transport. Three questions sort every case.
